processing: Leaves of the endemic Hawaiian shrub are harvested and dried, then sold crumbled or whole. Processing is typically minimal.
harvest_season: No prized picking is recorded; small growers harvest leaves as the plants allow.
appearance_dry: Crumbled dark olive-green dried leaf, sometimes with bits of stem.
taste_profile: Smooth and mild, faintly earthy, with a slightly sweet undertone.

brewing.notes: About 2 tablespoons of crumbled leaf to 2 cups of water just off the boil. Cover and steep 8 to 10 minutes; it does not turn bitter with a longer steep.

vintage_note: Sold by small Hawaiian growers with no vintage, typically as recently dried loose leaf or bags. Look for the name of the farm and island, because supply is local and limited. As with other dried leaf herbs, freshness counts more than age.
description:
Māmaki is a shrub found only in Hawaii, growing wild in the understorey of wet forests on all the main islands except Kahoʻolawe and Niʻihau. The tea comes from its leaves and contains no Camellia sinensis.

Processing is simple, essentially drying, which leaves a plain leaf infusion.

The cup is amber to rust in colour, smooth and quiet, with mild earthiness and a little sweetness. Give it a long, covered steep of 8 to 10 minutes; it has no bitter edge to fear.

Buy from named island growers if you can, and treat health claims on packaging with care. Anyone pregnant, nursing or on medication would do well to ask a doctor first.
history:
Native Hawaiians used the plant as medicine and for dye, and it is reported to have been drunk as a hot infusion, though detailed records are scarce and much of what circulates comes from sellers.

Commercial tea is a smaller, modern story. University of Hawaiʻi agricultural specialists have worked on finding higher-yielding, better-tasting varieties to expand the market.
